review:
What once was a very impressive little title has now turned into one of the biggest franchises for Square Enix and a Cult Favorite among the fans, so let's see how it all began shall we ?

In Just Cause we play as Rico Rodriguez. He is an agent sent in to the island San Esperito. Our mission is to kill a dictator Mendoza and free the island from his reign.

Back when this game came out I found it quite impressive. The Island is massive, but it doesn't matter cause there is nothing to see there. All of it is just a big jungle which all of it looks the same. There are small villages which act as outposts and you can clear them out.  The city is uninspiring and there's nothing to do there.

The gameplay is by far the weakest third person shooter I have ever seen. The shooting feels clunky and sometimes my shots don't even connect with the enemies, not to mention most guns are weak as hell, and the better weapons have low ammo counts.

The graphics (apart from the CGI cut scenes) are still great. The lush island is awesome and getting a boat and going through the rivers is really fun, but as stated before there's nothing to see, but it's still fun. 

The driving controls are some of the worst driving controls I have ever seen, they even top the driving controls in Watch Dogs. Since unlike in Just Cause 2 you can't travel with the grappling hook, so most of the time you will need to use vehicles.

The game also has side quests, but most of them are boring as hell and you can grind them since they never end. So if you want something more with the game after you're done you can do the mundane side quests.

The game took me 6 hours to finish, once the game is finished you can explore the island, but as stated before there's nothing to do there.

The game also has a major spike in difficulty in the final missions, so be prepared to be pissed off. 

Overall even though the game didn't age well, it's still fun to play for a bit, but it's the weakest in the series. In the end I will give this a positive review, but I still suggest playing Just Cause 2 instead.

Final Rating:
6/10 - Okay

First a word of caution: if you are expecting this game to be like Just Cause 2/3, don't get your hopes up!  This game is the pinnacle of early 2000's jankieness (despite releasing in 2006).  If your willing to look past the somewhat clunky controls and often repetitive gameplay, there is a lot of cheesy fun to be had, but also a lot of faults that players of the newer games will likely not be able to look past.

First off, this is an old game, so there are several things you need to do to make it play properly on a modern PC.
1.  Force the game to run in widescreen through Steam (just search for directions on how).
2.  Install the fan made patch that fixes the shadow effects in the game (you need to Steam version too, not the CD one, so check the thread in the Steam descusion board for a link)
3.  Lock the framerate of the game to a maximum of 60 FPS, more then that causes problems.  Ideally lock it at 30 FPS if you can stand it, as camera control and gun aiming isn't as slow then.  I did this through NVIDIA Control Panel, but you might have to find your own method.

Now for the review itself:
The plot of Just Cause 1 is, uh...  It's a Just Cause game, you play as Rico on a very cheesy adventure to take down the oppressive government of a fictional country (likely based on Cuba).  To do this you will perform story missions with hillariusly bad acting and cutsceenes with objectives that usually revolve around killing someone or blowing something up.  You can also do liberations as well as side missions for two different factions, but they are quite repetitive.  To occomplish these tasks, you will utilize a large collection of weapons, vehicles, and special abilities.  Among these special abilities are your parachute and (starting in story Mission 3) grapleing gun.  Unfortunently the grapleing gun in this game is far more limited then it is in the sequals.  You must switch to it like you do a normal weapon before using it, and it can only graple onto vehicles.  

Speaking of vehicles, there are quite a lot of them here: cars, boats, planes, helicopters, and even a couple armored vehicles.  Depending on the vehicle, the driving physics are often actually better then in Just Cause 2, though air vehicles are worse.  Helis expecially are exicuted rather poorly, with no straifing option, just up/down, forward/back, and rotate.  The game does have a very generus lock-on mechanic when in a vehicle though, which helps a bit.  Stunt position is in this game, but it really just serves as a quick way to jump to another vehicle and hijack it, as you cannot shoot in stunt possition.

On foot gunplay is pretty basic, with a large veriety of weapons, but they mostly feel the same.  Combat is just run and gun, no grapling hook combat, and no auto aim (though enemy hit boxes are quite generus).

There are a few interesting things you can do in this game that you actually can't do in Just Cause 2:
Hitchhicking: if you enter the passenger side of a vehicle and don't hit any buttons, you will ride along with the AI driving you.
Pilotless helis can stay airborn: if you go to the stunt position on a helicopter and then jump off, the helicopter will remain flying.  This is very useful if you just want to grab a collectable or something really quick but don't see a good place to land.

So if you are looking for a cheesy, somewhat broken, 2000's "GTA Clone," you could have a lot of fun with this game, but it really doesn't hold up at all compared to modern games.

Being something of a completionist when it comes to video game franchises, I wanted to introduce myself to the Just Cause games the proper way; by starting with the first one.

Now I'll keep this short. Frankly. after having completed the game. I'm baffled at the people who think it hasn't aged well. I regret never having been aware of this gem back in the PS2 era. or I would have definitely spent way more time in San Esperito than in San Andreas.

Graphics-wise. the game is gorgeous. I can only imagine what it must have looked like to players back when it released. Regarding gameplay, I genuinely think Just Casue 1 is a more fun game than GTA San Andreas. The freedom you're allowed with every single damn mission is amazing. GTA V doesn't have the freedom this game does. And everything else, from shooting to driving to flying to skydiving. feels great in my honest opinion. Rico was just as unstoppable back then as he is now.

Also, I read many people saying that the last mission of the game was extremely hard. I don't know about them, but I didn't find it any harder than any other mission I'd done. I've definitely died more to some other mission.

All in all, especially for the price it's always going for, highly recommended if you're into older games.
It feels like a proof-of-concept for stunts, with hints of what's to come. The sequels take that potential and run wild with it, so there's little reason to circle back to the first entry today.

If you follow Just Cause series, this is the OG one. This one really sets tone for Rico. I know it's old game, graphics low, repetitive music, physics compromized and all that. But looking at its release date, it performed good. It gets really hard sometimes, but you enjoy it after beating it and those cutscenes are cool af. I played Just Cause 2 first, but really wanted to try OG one. So did. Not a perfect start for the series, but perfect setup for upcoming masterpieces in the series.

Before you buy, consider..

- Limited resolution support

Game displays optional resolutions as low as 640x480 to 1600x1200, but only 1280x1024 is the max, selectable resolution for the game. And editing config files won't do crap for you.

To get your game to run in your monitor's native resolution, you're gonna need one of two versions of this program called res changer..

http://steamcommunity.com/app/6880/discussions/0/846959520923192823/

http://steamcommunity.com/app/6880/discussions/0/594821545181783362/

Version 1 or 2. Try 2 because it's newer. If it doesn't work, 1 might. 2 didn't work for me, so I had to use 1. Only drawback to having to use 1 is that it has no support for windowed mode like 2. And that alt-tabbing with 1 crashes your game. But, hey, it works. And I almost refunded my game. Looked awful downscaled. Game may be old, but still should have had more resolution support.

- Very few graphics settings.

You're gonna need to force AA, AF, etc on from your video driver control panel. Everything in menu only affects quality of textures, shadows, and post-processing FX.

Overall, the game is a good game. I have less than an hour on it over Steam, but I speak from experience from having played it on console years ago.

Pros: As GTA3 clones go, adding extreme sports and OTT stunts is one of the ideas that make it worthwhile, introducing things that you find yourself wishing were in GTA3. Tremendous freedom, with multiple approaches to two thirds of the main missions(parachute in, burst through the front, sneak in, etc.). If you're in a vehicle moving fast, or you make a vertical jump of about a dozen meters or more, you can engage your parachute, from where you can comfortably shoot or grapple to any vehicle. Shooting is like a proper third person shooter, not like GTA3 and Vice City. Vehicles include cars, motorcycles, boats, helicopters and planes, all of these types can come armed with machineguns and/or rockets, and all of them useful: sail, since you're in an island paradise, and going across water may be the shortest distance between two points; helicopter flight is easily the most flexible way to travel, because of mountains and sea; and planes are by far the fastest way to travel far. Control is great, no matter what you travel by. Fairly challenging. Limits on ammo and weapon carry capacity(two pistols, two types of C4, and another two guns - choose carefully between SMGs, assault and sniper rifles, RPGs and a grenade launcher) ensure that you are careful in shootouts. A fun arcade game.

Cons: Very clearly rushed, with glitches and bugs. Nothing to do once you've completed the short story and liberated all enemy zones and/or completed a certain number of the uninspired, crushingly inconsequential and repetitive side-missions. Characters are bland, and there's little to the story, meaning there's almost no "meat" to what's going on(the fun stuff is all in the game-play). Over half of the large island nation is forest and sea. Too many story missions are samey.

My recommendation: If you can live with its rather rough edges, this is among the most fun open-world games.

Nowhere even close to being as great as the second. But if your like me and have to play the whole series get ready for repetitve repetitve side mission and a okay main story. If you need a fun little time killer though, you found it.

[h1]Just cause you can play this, doesn't mean you should.[/h1]

After playing all three sequels, curiosity made me come back and try the game that started it all. And...

I don't mind older games, and a little jank doesn't stop me. But there are so many issues, small and big - yes, the game is playable. Yes, there are missions for you to do. Yes, the world is absolutely gigantic and doubtlessly has been an achivement for the time. But it's also the definition of an empty open world with nothing to do, a gigantic world that is more of a chore than pleasure to travel around and explore.

[h1]Major issues that have been solved by sequels:[/h1]

[list]
[*]The open world is pointless. Aside from randomly generated side missions, which consist of few repeating activities given by nameless NPCs, and useless "collectibles", there is nothing to do in it.
[*]The devs knew it, because the game has implemented fast travel in between the missions - that way, you can completely ignore the open world and just travel mission from mission, and after playing the game for few hours and trying to do the repetitive activities over and over, I would recommend that.
[*]Your grappling hook is terrible and most of the time pointless - they really improved it immensely in sequels, here, don't expect to ever really use it.
[*]You barely cause any mayhem and you barely destroy anything. None of the activities you know from sequels are here yet, all you can do outside of campaign is one repetitive type of "capture settlement" activity, and there are hundreds of them. You can also do absolutely pointless side missions, involving you bringing a vehicle, maybe shooting down a helicopter and such. You might do few, and then you will never bother again, seeing that those just repeat and any of the same quest NPCs all across the map will give them to you. It's like radiant quests, except worse. Even causing chaos isn't nowhere near as fun as in GTA, pedestrians randomly despawn and everything feels very wonky in general.
[*]So, so many smaller technical and design issues, that I don't even want to list everything. Sound engine is busted. You will be chased by cops and you will hear the sounds coming from a car behind you in front of you. It's that bad, I have never really seen anything like that. Eventually, you will feel like schizophrenic, just hearing random voices. Helicopters tend to randomly spawn and just follow you around the entire island, if you decide to capture some settlements. The AI is as primitive as it gets, and there is very little variety to anything. Vehicles having barely any physics - a jeep can easily push around a tank. 
[*]Some missions are okay, some are terrible. Story is fine in concept, but barely there. Bad guy has no personality. Rico has no personality besides being Antonio Banderas knockoff. Few "supporting" characters barely exist, making the campaign feel fragmented, just a set of random missions that lead to bad guy's doom. And I could go on...
[/list]

[h1]Want to play it?[/h1]

Nothing in the game is absolutely terrible, but there are so many better games to play. I kept getting feeling of sunk cost fallacy at any point I've engaged in the open world, instead of just playing another campaign mission. The gameplay just isn't interesting enough.

There are no skills, no perks, nothing practical to unlock by ranking with the two friendly factions. Everything you need gets unlocked from the campaign hideouts. Perhaps a proper remake could be great. Because the premise has always been good, but the execution is lame.

Ultimately, this is just a promise of what would be. Just Cause 1 crawled, so Just cause 2 and 3 could run, and Just Cause 4 could limply walk.

★ I wrote this review to help you decide whether you can get [b] YOUR MONEY'S & TIME'S WORTH [/b] from this game.

[h1] TL;DR [/h1]
★ I only recommend buying this game when it’s on sale or included in a bundle. It’s far from perfect but it can be a nice little addition to your library with the discounted price. I recommend it because liberating settlements and doing silly things on a huge map is enjoyable.

[h1] SUMMARY [/h1]
★ You are a Latin field operative trying to overthrow a corrupt government on a large island. The gameplay mostly revolves around liberating settlements to fulfil that purpose (and jumping from vehicle to vehicle while making cheesy sentences). The story is not rich or long. The environment is rather empty. Side quests become repetitive. You can come up with your unique gameplay style with the use of grappling hook but the grappling hook in this game is inferior to the ones in other games of this series. The resolution options of the game are very limited. There are a wide variety of vehicles in the game. Controls are limited and not smooth. There are no difficulty options.
★ More reviews like this: https://steamcommunity.com/groups/usefulreviews

[h1] STORY (Nothing special) [/h1]
★ You are a Latin field operative working for the Agency and you are sent to a large island to overthrow a corrupt government and eliminate any weapons of mass destruction you find. 
♦ You got two support agents who brief you and give you the necessary vehicle(s), if any, for your next mission. You have to meet up with these people at the beginning of each story mission.
★ The story isn't rich or long.
♦ There are two factions on this island that require your help as the protagonist. Rebel forces, namely the guerrilla and a drug cartel. You help these two factions fight against the government (plus its mercenaries) and a rival cartel respectively.
♦ You don’t speak much but make cheesy sentences and mention your self control issues here and there.

[h1] GAMEPLAY (Repetitive and clunky but also amusing) [/h1]
♦ It's a third person sandbox game.
★ You can approach the missions and the game in general in any way you want. With the use of grappling hook you can come up with slightly different gameplay styles.
♦ You are given a PDA that allows you to check the map, the political map, extraction points, current mission information, relations with the two factions, statistics and order a heavy drop.
♦ The island has 34 provinces. These provinces' political situation are shown in the political map. These provinces are all government stable at the beginning of the game. As you progress through the campaign these provinces will become politically unstable meaning you can go to settlements in these provinces, talk to the guerrilla waiting near these settlements and start a liberation for that particular settlement. If you go to these provinces while they are government stable the guerrilla there will only offer side quests. As you liberate settlements for guerrilla in a particular province, you will progressively control that province to the point when the province becomes guerrilla stable.
♦ Government control doesn't affect cartel conflicts.
♦ Liberation missions earn you reputation for the faction you are helping and follow the same mechanics for the most of the time. You push back enemy forces (by destroying structures of interest or killing enemy forces) till you liberate the settlement (by capturing their flag or eliminating the person of interest). Losing too much men too quickly fails the liberation.
♦ If you gain enough reputation with a faction you will get promoted. Guerilla give you safe houses, vehicles and weapons based on your rank. Drug cartel gives you vehicles and safe houses based on your rank.
★ Side quests are pretty generic, don't give much reputation and become repetitive.
♦ There are collectibles scattered across the map. These are shown on the map with blue dots and give reputation when acquired.
★ You can't upgrade your health and can't improve unlocked weapons.
★ You have a grappling hook which is basically a high-powered magnet harpoon. It can only stick to vehicles. You can jump from vehicle to vehicle, grapple onto a vehicle and follow it with a parachute. It has limited functionality compared to the grappling hooks in other Just Cause games.
♦ Enemies have a chance to drop medkits during missions. Other than that you have to go to safe houses to replenish your health. Safe houses also provide weapons, ammo and save stations. You can only save your game in these locations.
♦ As the field operative you can have the agency send a helicopter to extract (fast travel) you to one of the unlocked safe houses on the map. You can also have that very same helicopter drop one of four vehicles in a crate from the sky. These are the Gryocopter (basically a tiny helicopter with the size of a motorcycle), a jeep, a motorcycle and an advanced watercraft that looks like batmobile. If you stay at the drop zone you might die because gravity is a thing.
♦ No matter where you are you hear the police saying things like "Stop citizen! This is the police!" and "Halt citizen!" as if you hear voices in your head.
♦ Weapon, vehicle and on foot controls aren't smooth.
♦ You can't sprint.
♦ Enemies jump when they are killed.
♦ There are no difficulty options.
♦ Enemies die rather easily but you mostly don't. Your biggest weakness is being hit by a vehicle. (Which almost always kills you.)
♦ When you wish to be extracted to one of the unlocked safe houses i believe it's time consuming to select a safe house as you can't just hover your mouse over them on the map. There are corresponding safe house names on the left (such as Agency01, Agency02...) and when you select a name the corresponding safe house starts flashing on the map (all safe houses are represented with the same icon). If you don't know the name of the safe house to which you want to be extracted you will have to go through names one by one until the desired safe house starts flashing.
♦ There are numerous vehicles you can make use of. You unlock more as you progress in the game.

[h1] ENVIRONMENT (Huge but empty) [/h1]
★ The map is huge but mostly filled with mountains, trees and roads. The settlements are rather spaced out and there are small structures here and there. All in all, exploration isn't rewarded and it may take a while to get to your destination without the use of extraction.

[h1] VISUALS (Outdated and saturated) [/h1]

[h1] TECHNICAL (Limited resolution but runs smoothly) [/h1]
★ I personally did not come across (or did not notice at the very least) any bad optimization.
★ The highest screen resolution the game offers is [b]1600x1200[/b] but i believe most people use the 1280x1024 option (which is the second highest). You can enter this [b]"/width=x /height=y"[/b] in your game's launch options (right click the game and select properties) with x and y being the desired resolutions. Bear in mind that this might mess up your minimap. You can also either look for guides explaining how to edit the game's files or download a fix from the web.
★ [b]Save files[/b] are located in: [b]%documents%\JustCause\saves[/b]. (I believe it's always a good idea to backup your save files.)
♦ You might encounter a bug regarding shadows. If that happens you can check the general discussion with the name "Fix for the 'creeping shadows' bug!".

[h1] MODS AND SUCH (Only a few)[/h1]
★ I have come across only a few mods for this game.
♦ You can look up OmniFX Preset (Vibrant) if you wish to enhance the visuals of your game.

Just Cause is an old game, originally released for (and for me, played on) the PS2. It is clunky, starts freezing up if you keep it on too long without saving, has (compared to modern games) terrible graphics, sound design, and story. The voice acting is mediocre at best, and the game is severely lacking in many areas (such as describing game mechanics, for one) which we take for granted in modern games.
But you know what? It's FUN. There are guns and explosions and the cars can't be controlled in mid-air, and things blow up for seemingly no reason sometimes; if you stand in the road and do nothing chaos ensues around you, you can punch an AI and then they'll punch another AI (why???). This game is, by modern standards, broken, flawed, and bad. But I don't care. Because when I play this, I'm reminded of a simpler time, where games didn't have to be complicated to be great to play. And that's why I love this game.

In my opinion, Just Cause is one of the best games of the mid-2000s. It should be in there with classics like Half Life 2, Saints Row, Doom 3, Tomb Raider Legend and GTA San Andreas. The amount of fun you can have is endless. Sure, the island is at least 90 percent trees, but when you're flying a plane during a sunrise or along the coast, the game looks gorgeous. 


The story, even though the start and end cutscenes are FMV sequences, and the in the in-game cutscenes, characters' lips barely move when they are talking, is pretty insane with the amount of action there is, from blowing up a nuclear power plant, to assassinating Mendoza's (the dictator you take down) sons, the story is solid for this kind of game, though short. 

The graphics, however, are comparably worse than a lot of other games of 2006, especially with Crysis coming out a year later. But, I think the graphics fit the art style for the game. 

The game's physics are okay? Many people complain about the lacking realistic GTA-style physics, but first of all, why are you driving? The map is so huge, why don't you just go to your neighborhood airport and take a plane? The driving physics are ... fine. It feel very arcade-y but it feel good to drive around. They could be better, but if you're using a fast car racing down a highway, it should be no problem. 

The map is huge (around 1000km^2) , getting across it in a motorcycle or a car is impossible. Also, there is very little varied terrain. It's either forest or flat plains before a forest. Also, the forest is littered with immovable trees and rocks which will either stop your car and you have to reverse, or send you flying if you're on a motorbike. 

The liberation missions are the best part of this game. Liberating a village or a Montano-controlled cartel house is amazing. You can drop in a MV to blast your way through everything, or you could just gun everybody down with a machinegun. The game has a whole array of weapons, from the default Pitbulls, to the Nova 9 SMG, to the Mako Hammerhead grenade launcher. Also the ability to shoot grenades in midair is key to destruction. Sure, the explosions are quite unrealistic for the modern times, but it is beautiful to look at. But after the mission Guadalicano Choo Choo, the game gets extremely tough during liberations, in which Black Hand terrorists replace the police or the army, and even during Montano liberations, they start using more shotguns, and a helicopter with missiles. This does get frustrating quickly as you keep dying, but the key is to keep moving. The copters can't hit you as much, if you're moving! This is when the RPGs or the Grenade Launchers are useful. Also, when you're liberating big cities or military bases, this still is in effect. RPGS and grenade launchers are a must, but also keep moving. DO NOT GET INTO ANY VEHICLES, during these liberations, because then the tanks and helicopters will bombard you with shells and missiles so quickly, your vehicle will explode and kill you before you can say "Viva la Revolucion!" Destroy all the enemy tanks you see, (not all, don't waste ammo), but try getting one of your own. But, sometimes going on foot can help you see even more action. Tossing grenades, missiling everybody, and gunning enemies down is so fun, it's probably the best part of this game.

Also, don't come in to contact with any moving vehicles, because even if you're not getting run over, you still lose health, and when you do get run over, you could lose up to 75 percent of your health. This can become tricky during liberation missions. Also, the enemy AI, if they are in a vehicle, will sometimes beeline towards you, so just be careful for that.

Also, Rico Rodriguez (who's is literally a different person in each game) is a fitting protagonist for the game. He is very young in this game, though in Just Cause 4, he is at least 40. Also, his rare one-liners are pretty cool.

This game's soundtracks is one of the best I've ever heard. The Spanish style music with some modern American beats give this all the more reason to play this game. When you're driving down the freeway and the police and a helicopter chase you, and you hear the amazing music... feels good man.

Overall, I'd totally recommend this game for its arcade-iness. The amazing Just Cause series started from this, and you have to give this game credit. But you'll probably have to get over some obstacles to enjoy it.

Just Cause has become a series renowned for its massive open worlds and explosive action that would leave Micheal Bay impressed. The developers, Avalanche Studios, have become full on triple-A developers thanks to their series of summer blockbuster simulators, but they had humble beginnings.

Anyone familiar with this franchise will not be surprised by the plot; The tyrannical Salvador Mendoza, a man believed to be in possession of weapons of mass destruction, has taken over the fictional South American island nation of San Esperito.  Because of this, Rico Rodriguez, who has now become a staple of the series, is sent to the country to aid the rebels who reside there in overthrowing Mendoza and to take out the president's corrupt government officials. This gives the title of the game an often overlooked double meaning, as "Just Cause" can be interpreted as Rico's actions being honorable or as a shortened version of "Just because", the perfect answer as to why you a do any of the over-the-top things the game allows you to.

Those who have played later games in the series but not this one may take while to adjust to the gameplay. Many of the major elements of games to come are still present -- the massive game map is littered with races, side-quests, and villages to liberate. However, the game itself plays much differently, mostly due to the less fleshed-out stunt system. This game's grappling hook is still fun to use, but it can only latch onto vehicles, meaning that travelling by using the parachute and hook as many players did in JC2 is not possible. Thankfully, you're able to request a vehicle drop at your location whenever you're not in a pursuit. As you liberate more villages and bases, more vehicles become unlocked. My biggest issue with the unarmed vehicles in the game is that you can't use weapons while you're riding on top of them, making on-road vehicular combat needlessly frustrating. While in pursuits, I often had to abandon my car every several minutes and climb into a police or military one due to taking significant damage because I was unable to defend myself without heavily reducing my mobility.

Liberating settlements also works quite differently then it did in later games. You start a liberation by speaking to the rebel or gang member outside the settlement, and both sides will immediately begin to call in reinforcements. There are three barricades that must be destroyed in every settlement (that are really easy to get around and could hardly be considered barricades, but "logic" and Just Cause are an oxymoron), and the enemies will suddenly disappear once you either capture the flag or take out a gang leader depending on which type of settlement you're overthrowing. These battles feel incredibly intense due to the large number of NPCs. I was frequently getting hit by bullets I had no hope of avoiding, but this was never too much of an issue since enemies will occasionally drop medkits upon defeat. The scale of these shootouts is impressive, and the number of weapons dropped by combatants on the ground that I would see in the aftermath of liberations never failed to impress me. This game was released before the open-world shooter formula was refined, and the game can sometimes feel even more repetitious than modern Ubisoft titles, and if you don't enjoy those types of games, you certainly won't enjoy this one. However, I don't mind very much when the repetitious activities are so entertaining.

It's difficult to notice that this game's AI opponents don't live up to the "intelligence" part of the acronym when you're fighting them on foot in large groups, but things get ugly when vehicles are involved. You'll often see massive pileups of cars in the middle of villages after liberating them, and the enemies are just as reckless on the open road. They would frequently ram me off of cliffs and took themselves down with me, and would also often run into lampposts and trees. The enemies don't cease their stupidity while airborne, either; the helicopter pilots may be able to shoot you from incredible distances even through thick trees and vegetation, but they usually stay still and will never attempt to avoid your gunfire when you're on foot, making them incredibly easy targets if you've got a rocket launcher equipped.

As for the campaign missions, they're okay, but mostly forgettable. There are a few fairly fun moments I can recall, but what I most remember are the numerous glitches I came across and frustrations that arose from them and the ludicrous saving system. Some of the more notable bugs I ran into were when tanks tumbled around uncontrollably when I drove them, triggered explosives bouncing across the ground when I deployed them, objective items disappearing upon retrying levels, and the game instantly crashing on PC if the game was in anyway minimized. I once accidentally pressed the Windows key while piloting a helicopter when I meant to lower the vehicle by holding the nearby CTRL key. As a result, the game crashed and I lost nearly half an hour of progress. (This apparently doesn't affect Windows XP users, but if you own a PC running an operating system from 2001, it's probably factory-built and has no hope of smoothly running this game) "Why didn't you just manually save?" you might be asking. Well, the only way to save your progress in Just Cause is via prompts that appear when you complete a campaign mission or if you use a control panel at one of the safehouses you unlock as you liberate San Esperito. This combined with the inability to start the game up from mission checkpoints caused me to become stuck for long periods of time on some segments of the game.

Just Cause is one of the most polarizing games I've played in awhile. The gameplay has thrilling highs and extremely frustrating lows; the islands are densely packed with well-detailed vegetation and foliage, but the FMV cutscenes are grainy and ugly; the flamenco soundtrack does wonders to accentuate the action, but the voice acting is hilariously bad. The game may have many shortcomings, but they are ultimately overshadowed by the often entertaining action. It's far from a masterpiece, but it's worth checking out if you want to kill time with some open-world silliness.

FINAL SCORE: 7.2 \ 10, might play again.

This was my first introduction to open-world type games, and I have to say that I'm hooked now.  But what about THIS game?

Well, I can say that despite a few hilarious glitches (some of which a player can take advantage of, while continuing to laugh), and the occasional silly graphics moments, this is a game worth playing once, waiting a few years, and playing again.  There's so much to do, and so many ways to do it.  The battle scenes will get your adrenaline up, and death moments will give you that sudden comedown feeling, while victory moments are eerily quiet and oddly normal after all that chaos.  You'll want that cerveza fria that some guy is selling (oddly, moments after a battle is over, and likely from a stand that you might have accidentally blown up with a tank a few minutes before that).

Aircraft are fun to fly, whether skimming over treetops or through the clouds.  Tanks, cars, and motorcycles require you to be careful with the throttles and steering.  Boats...well, let's just say you can spend hours on the water doing nothing at all, just for the heck of it.  And remember, this is a huge open world; conquer it, and it's all yours.  What you haven't conquered may decide to fight you back, and that could be fun in its own right.

I had plenty of runs on foot across whole islands--the equivalent of MILES of running--while helicopters chased me with guns blazing, state police flying off the road trying to ram me through the trees...and armed only with two pistols.  It's easy to get lost, too, and the map takes some getting used to.  Imagine running from a horde of guys, and suddenly coming out of the trees and up to a cliff!  Luckily, you can jump, fall a bit, and parachute to the ground, avoiding everyone except the helicopters.  Run to a safe house or friendly territory, and you just might get away while the enemy are forced to fight others just for the chance to keep chasing you.  That's why gaining territory is important.

There are some cringeworthy aspects to the game.  To be honest, the whole banana republic politics aspect could be viewed as problematic by some.  I'd say they forget that the hero character is Hispanic, like the NPCs and enemies of the islands.  I didn't care for the cheesy, big-jawed John-Wayne-in-a-CIA-issue-Hawaiian-shirt character, and the easy-on-the-eyes blonde lady working with him didn't make the stereotypes any easier to view.  Then again, I could be taking all the satire a bit too seriously--LMAO!

There's one more thing I should add.  As of this review, I have NOT played GTA games (I didn't have anything to play them on back when they were out).  The closest I could compare this game to is Driver 3 or Parallel Lines (the latter of which I never got to finish).  Driver 3 is NOT open world, but felt immense and immersive in a very similar way, to the point that I am now forever ready to visit Nice and Istanbul (I've already been to Miami, and I'm not sure about Rio yet).  If you enjoyed Driver 3, you WILL enjoy Just Cause, and find yourself wishing that the Driver games were more like this.  That said, you can go full-on Tanner anywhere in these islands, so have at it.

All that to say this:  just get this game already!

ADDENDUM:  A few years and a few games later, I'm still waxing nostalgic over this game.  It is truly one of the best ever.  I still recommend it, especially to gaming novices.  Have fun!

Explosive Freedom with a Tether of Frustration

Diving into Just Cause is like strapping into a chaotic action movie where you're both the hero and the stunt coordinator. Set in the sun-drenched fictional archipelago of San Esperito, this open-world sandbox leans hard into style over subtlety—and for the most part, that’s exactly what makes it memorable.

The biggest draw here is pure, unfiltered freedom. You're Rico Rodriguez, a suave operative armed with an endless supply of gadgets, vehicles, and skydiving gear. The game lets you skydive onto moving cars, hijack helicopters mid-flight, and zip across the landscape using your iconic grappling hook. These over-the-top stunts, even by today’s standards, feel gleefully ridiculous. There’s a definite charm to how the game encourages you to blow things up just for the thrill of it.

The map is massive—lush jungles, winding coastal roads, and bustling military outposts dot the landscape, all inviting you to experiment. That scope is both a strength and a weakness. On one hand, there’s always something to do: liberating villages, sabotaging military installations, or just causing general mayhem with a tank you borrowed. On the other hand, the map can feel artificially bloated. Large portions of the world serve little purpose, offering little interaction or variation beyond the scenery.

The mission design is where the cracks begin to show. Despite the freedom offered elsewhere, main objectives are repetitive and often feel like slight variations of the same formula: drive here, blow this up, escape. Side missions, while abundant, suffer from the same copy-paste design philosophy. There's a real missed opportunity in how little the story and characters engage with the world’s chaos. Rico himself has the personality of an action figure pulled off the shelf—cool, confident, but hollow.

Technically, the game is a mixed bag. For its time, the visuals held up decently, with tropical backdrops that look surprisingly good from high altitudes. But on closer inspection, texture pop-ins, stiff animations, and dated effects are unavoidable. Controls can also be janky, especially when driving or aiming, which adds a layer of frustration when the action ramps up.

Still, the undeniable fun comes from moments where the game stops trying to be structured and lets you write your own brand of insanity. Jumping from a plane, grappling to a passing car mid-air, and slingshotting onto a rooftop with rockets firing in the background—these are the moments that make Just Cause feel unique, even today.

Pros:
Huge open world that encourages creative chaos

Grappling hook and stunts offer real freedom of movement

Fun, over-the-top action that rarely takes itself seriously

Tropical setting is vibrant and inviting

Cons:
Repetitive mission structure with shallow objectives

Weak narrative and flat characters

Clunky controls and outdated mechanics

Large areas of the map feel underutilized

Final Verdict: 7/10

Just Cause is far from perfect, but it’s a blast when it embraces its absurdity. If you can look past the shallow missions and technical quirks, there’s a whole lot of fun to be had in the sky, on the road, or wherever your next explosion takes you.

Just Cause is a good game, one of the best in the series. It has many pros, but also many cons. Its story is full of action, satire, and chaos. Its missions are varied and don't unnecessarily drag out the game. Then there's its beautiful map—it's fascinating how massive and well-crafted it is for the time it was released. Keep in mind it's almost twenty years old, and yet many of its mechanics have aged very well, just like the game itself.

However, the game also has many problems. The most noticeable for Spanish speakers is that when you start the game, it automatically defaults to English. Of course, with some file tweaks, it can be fixed. But this shouldn't happen in the first place.

Another issue, which I found maddening, is the imbalance with enemies. The helicopters are broken—they're infinitely superior to the player. Even if you focus on destroying them, they just keep spawning. Because that's another problem: the endless spawning of enemies. And I mean literally endless. They give you no breathing room—as soon as you kill one, four more appear. This makes completing objectives very difficult. The player is also at a disadvantage when it comes to vehicles, as they are clunky to drive and easily destroyed. I've needed 3-4 cars just to reach an objective. While all the enemies are shooting at you from their cars, helicopters, or boats, you can't do the same. This is especially frustrating in chase or extraction missions, as your vehicles always get destroyed. Even armored cars have the durability of a watermelon.

Other than that, the game is great. It's fun and unique.

Ok, so... wow. I came to this game last, after having played 2 to 4 already. This game is... a real mixed bag, and there's more to dislike than there is to like about it, especially now (yes, I'm sure that if I played this in 2006 when it came out it would have blown my mind). But as time moves on, games age. Just Cause has aged like milk. There are aspects I enjoyed, especially the parallels to be drawn with mechanics introduced in later games - but the main reason I picked this one up was to get a look at the grappling hook, something that has stood the test of time and become almost synonymous with the Just Cause series. And... holy hells. It's treated as a weapon, just with infinite ammunition, and can only grapple to other vehicles and have them drag you along. It just feels weird after seeing the grapple evolve across the other games, even though I know I should have expected something this clunky from the first game because... y'know, that's how evolution works. And speaking of weapons... man the gunplay in this game is something else. It feels so bland and dead, and unfortunately this is not a point that can be held against the excuse of "but it's from 2006!". I think this might actually be the worst gunplay I have ever experienced. Finally, the world itself - we don't talk about the storyline in Just Cause, it's cheesy and it's a little too on-the-nose and that's what makes it Just Cause - but San Esperito just feels too bland and same-y. It's like if the first level of Far Cry was stretched out to cover the full island, but they just stretched what they had rather than put more things in the space. It's very empty, even the cities that do exist feel like simply lifeless grey blocks. Considering later titles in the series, especially 2 and 4, this feels like a completely bizarre starting point to then go on and create Panau from.

This game slaps like no other, however, if you learn to study the game itself, both as a starting point for the evolution of the series, and for an engaging (and surprisingly still available) example of the gaming world of the dark past of 2006. An open world of this scale at this time? Unprecedented. Vehicles lying, like, [u] everywhere[/u] that you could use to actually traverse this open world? Almost inconceivable. Useless collectables scattered across every island of this open world? Hells, I'm sure if I could get past how awful Rico's face looked compared to Just Cause 4, I'm sure I'd have loved picking up every single godsdamn one of them. However, if you're playing for the reason, "I want to have fun playing a game", then this is not the game for you.

The biggest Open world environment to date… Numerous guns to choose from, dressed in all black and ready to unleash hell… You are in for a world of fun!

Some key points that this game offers:

1.	The Avalanche Engine™ at its best.
2.	More than 250 000 acres to explore, the biggest game area to date.
3.	A massive single player campaign.
4.	Even more side missions and other to dos.
5.	Ground, water and air travel!

Gameplay & Controls:

The game runs absolutely beautifully, fun and smooth as smooth can get. This is across all platforms; the hardware runs the game environment very well with no lag and near instant loading time to ensure that we have one constant action packed experience.

To describe Just Cause, I’d say it is in the same essence as Grand Theft Auto, however here you are pretty much the good guy. You have the same Open World environment feel that we have with GTA, but as I mentioned Just Cause is the biggest game to date with a massive game environment spread out across several Tropical Islands for us to explore.

Our main goal in Just Cause is to overthrow the corrupt government of San Esperito.  Rico Rodriguez is our protagonists name; he is a Latin Black Ops agent tasked with helping the rebels overthrow the Corrupt government.

The game world is divided up into small regions that start out being controlled by the government and as you progress through the game, You unlock side quests that allow you to take over control of these regions. In doing so you are rewarded with loyalty points and the higher the points go the more weapons, safe houses and vehicles you unlock. 

Graphics:

Drop dead gorgeous! The game is really beautiful, no matter from which angle you look at it. Whether you are in or under the water, the ocean and its various colour schemes are truly a marvel to look at.

The islands may all look alike but they are unique in their own rights; whether it is the small cities and villages that occupy them or the way that the landscaping was done, it is all a visual splendour to enjoy and play in.
There are a wide variety of vehicles and weapons, all uniquely designed to ensure you can enjoy the variety that the game offers. Variety is the spice of life after all!

Character design is on par here as well, whether it is the random NPC’s that just fill the world or the quest givers, they are all beautifully crafted for our entertainment.

Under the settings panel are several options that can be adjusted for PC users.

Sounds:

Just as stunningly done as the rest of the game, whether it is the background sounds that makes the islands come alive, or the industrial sounds produced by the variety of vehicles on the road.

Everything has its own unique and beautiful tune. Character voice overs were done just as well, the accents fit well and the character behaviours are in sync with the sounds, again adding to the already high quality experience we have here.

The background music is superb, it makes things so much more fun, whether our ride blew up and we are forced to hike 2 km or we are chasing down a bad guy, the sound will be there to build the atmosphere and improve your experience.
We have full volume control under the settings panel.

Replayability:

Just Cause may not offer much in terms of new game plus mode or anything, but this game world is so massive and filled with so many side quests and other to dos that it will keep you just as busy as a game with a new game plus feature.

MGR Gaming’s Conclusions:
Spoilers ahead:

When it comes down to the numbers, Just Cause has been gorgeously crafted and masterfully presented, delivering a very high quality game that will ensure we have dozens of enjoyable hours behind it.

There is so much in this game, to see, explore and enjoy that it can’t be mentioned in mere words, it has to be experienced by playing the game yourself, and doing so will ensure that you have the time of your life.

In Just Cause you play as Rico, a most luminescent CIA spook who specializes in overthrowing Latin American governments. He's basically special agent doble sero siete. His friends, Bruce Campbell from burn notice and Tanya from Command and Conquer give him missions to fuck shit up in whatever fake country you are in. The game lets you fly through the main campaign, and it took me about 5 hours to plow through with a little screwing around on the side.

The missions are what you would come to expect from a game of this not quite GTA genre, kill this guy, blow that up, steal this, and so on. Each main mission led in with an abrupt cutscene describing what heinous shit you were about to get into, and often ended with one as well. The main missions were pretty varied and fairly fun. There were a few too many "on rails, in the back on the gun" missions though. There were also side missions you could do to grind relation points, which were shorter and more fetch quest, busywork-ish. Once the main missions in an area were completed, you could then also start liberation missions in which you and your rebel and narco friends try to overthrow the local government or cartel. These started out fun, but were very cookie cutter and grew tiresome fairly quickly. 

You can see the groundwork for something special in the gameplay, but it's all too bare bones or poorly implemented in this first installation of the game. The grappling hook is there, but it's a separate weapon slot that is very inconvenient to use and abuse. The parachuting is cool but also controls clunky. The guns all feel samey and definitely have a linear progression of power, but the weapons slots are limited like many games of the time. There were two separate wanted levels for the government and the cartel, but you don't have any choice as far as who you work for, befriend or piss off. The large variety of vehicles on air land and sea were all pretty cool. The collectibles scattered around the map, yet another genre staple, are there as well but all they give you are some more faction favor as far as I could tell.

The thing that detracted the most from the game was the incredibly short range at which vehicles and people spawn around you. We're talking maybe a 200 foot circle around you where cars and people phase into and out of existence it seemed, which made the higher wanted level parts of the game a complete slog. The spawn radius felt tighter than GTA3 and that game is five years older. 

I did enjoy how little they tried to rationalize what you were doing throughout the story. They don't bother explaining how the big bad is a monster and cruel to his people and committing genocide and blah blah blah so that 'Merica can be the good guy, the CIA is just destabilizing this country for whatever reason it wants. Half of the mission briefings went something like "Kill this guy, that will make people miserable and revolt!", "Blow this up, that will piss off the populace!", "Steal this money for the CIA!", which is probably a more honest take than other games. Likewise I thought it was on the nose funny that your allies were a bunch of Che Guevara commies and a fucking drug cartel. 

Overall I think that even if I had played this in '06 it would be a let down to my nostalgia. If you're a huge JC fan and you want to see how far the series has come it might be worth a playthrough, but I don't believe you would really be missing anything by not playing it.

Liberation missions are a touch more interesting, since you're freeing a settlement from the goverment with other rebels, but these too become boring quickly.

Completing these activities earns you point with the respective faction and unlocks new vehicles and weapons at specific milestones. but I never bothered with them.

Developed by Avalanche Studios and published by the revered Eidos Interactive, Just Cause is an action oriented sandbox third-person shooter that takes place in San Esperito; a tropical island located in the Caribbean. Players control suave Agency operative Rico Rodriguez, who is called to the island to help overthrow its dictator, Salvador Mendoza. Overall, the story is one that entails a growing revolutionary resistance, wars with drug cartels, and a fascist government. In short, it's your typical action-packed Spanish anarchist tale, doused with just the right amount of dark humor.

Although the story has a multitude of creative missions that will suck you in right from the start, the game can be completed in 5-6 hours; if you take your time to max out your gang reputation, compete in races, and liberate strongholds, you'll end up getting around 7-10 hours of play time. Though one would be hard pressed to tediously grind out gang reputation through the game's side missions, since they're mostly comprised of repetitious fetch quests. The only benefit to leveling up the two available reputations are the unlocks that are offered when you get promoted, though in the end the monotony is not really worth the hassle. Sadly, this trait ultimately ends up making the sandbox of Just Cause a lost cause, as players are better off sticking to the primary missions.

The game also seems to suffer from inconsistent difficulty in many areas, and for some reason even if your heat level (much like the wanted level in Grand Theft Auto) is low, it seems like every cop and gang member in the area is right on your heels within a matter of seconds. Any mission that requires you to transport a vehicle from point A to point B without exploding due to bullet and missile damage can become infuriating; actually, any mission at all that ends in failure if your vehicle explodes.

A couple of features that really set this title apart from other sandbox games at the time it was released is the ability to freefall and parachute after jumping from a high altitude, as well as Rico's grapple hook gadget; both mechanics have since become a series staple. Unfortunately, the grapple hook in this release is completely useless due to poor controls, and the fact that you can only grapple onto a moving vehicle. During your stay on the island of San Esperito, you will also be able to drive cars and fly helicopters; the latter of which was a huge deal for a sandbox title back in 2006. Though, again, the controls and physics make maneuvering these vehicles troublesome. In fact, the entire control scheme of Just Cause is aged, and thus the game feels cumbersome.

Just Cause has its share of good moments, but it also has a conglomeration of down sides as well. On one hand, most of the missions are fun and inspired, and the action is enthralling. On the other hand, the game lacks depth, the side missions are a write off, the physics are bad, and the control system is clunky. There's also an issue with inconsistent difficulty, as some missions are terribly easy, while others are frustratingly hard; namely, any one that requires you to take a vehicle from one point to another and have it survive a barrage of missiles and bullets. Also be aware that if you want to play in your native resolution, you will need a third-party patch to do so. All in all, save yourself a few hours and just watch the 30 minute cutscene clip on YouTube to get yourself caught up with the story.
